compare_blocks.title: One-minute comparison

compare_blocks.body:
Imagine two subtitle editors who both keep an alternative line available before final review. A preference for openness can fit that choice, and so can a project brief that asks for options.

The shared P describes an approach to the outside world. In type dynamics, it means both profiles use an outward-facing perceiving function. Both can follow a glossary, meet a deadline and decide which line to submit.

The differing letters concern separate questions: where attention goes, which information stands out and what carries weight in a judgment. Someone can check a detail privately or discuss an abstract connection with colleagues.

### ### ESFP and INTP: weighing two ways to adapt the same pun

In a fictional kitchen scene, a character holds up a plate of food and says, “I’m a hot dish.” The joke links the literal hot meal with the character calling himself attractive. Two editors have the same footage and dialogue. Both need a one-line subtitle that can be read in about two seconds, with no room for a note.

For an English-language illustration, compare “I’m quite a catch” with “I’m the dish of the day.” The first makes the boast clear but loses the food image. The second keeps the food image and lets the shot carry part of the joke, but it may be less immediately clear as a boast.

One line of inquiry is what viewers could see and hear at the moment the line appears. Another is the connection between the two meanings and how a different phrase could recreate it. These illustrate S/N under the same conditions.

Either editor can check timing and look for another way to connect the meanings. Familiarity with the film, the intended audience and what the scene needs to communicate may guide the approach.

Show the alternatives to a few colleagues who have not seen the source. Ask what they understood and whether the line felt natural. Record those answers separately. The feedback can inform this edit and gives no evidence about a personality type.

### ### ESFP and INTP: how the two function stacks fit together

Both types have P, which points to an outward-facing perceiving function. For ESFP, S makes that function Se and E makes it dominant, supported by inward-facing Fi. For INTP, N makes the outward function Ne and I makes it auxiliary to inward-facing dominant Ti.

Under the convention used here, the stacks are Se–Fi–Te–Ni and Ti–Ne–Si–Fe. Pairing by family gives different orientations: Se with Si, Ni with Ne, Te with Ti, and Fi with Fe. The full order is different as well. In particular, ESFP’s dominant function takes in information and INTP’s dominant function evaluates it in the model.

The Foundation lists Thinking (Te or Ti) for ESFP’s tertiary function and Sensing (Se or Si) for INTP’s. Using Ti for ESFP or Se for INTP would produce an overlap with the other type’s dominant function. Function order does not set an order of action. comparison.summary:
ESFP and INTP share Perceiving (P) and differ on Extraversion and Introversion (E/I), Sensing and Intuition (S/N), and Thinking and Feeling (T/F). In Myers-Briggs type dynamics, both have an outward-facing perceiving function. ESFP’s Se is dominant, while INTP’s Ne supports its inward-facing dominant Ti.

- **E/I.** ESFP’s E describes a preference for directing attention and energy outward. INTP’s I describes a preference for directing them inward. Neither preference tells you how much someone speaks.
- **S/N.** ESFP’s S emphasises concrete details and experience. INTP’s N emphasises patterns, connections and possibilities. Both can draw on the same material.
- **T/F.** ESFP’s F emphasises values and effects on people. INTP’s T emphasises logical consistency and criteria that apply across cases. Either person can weigh both.

Under the convention used here, ESFP is Se–Fi–Te–Ni and INTP is Ti–Ne–Si–Fe. The two displayed stacks contain no identical abbreviations. The Myers & Briggs Foundation lists alternative tertiary orientations that can change which labels overlap.

Either person can read a subtitle aloud, analyse a pun or revise a line before delivery. The deadline, the material and who reviews it may shape the order. One action cannot identify a type.

compare_blocks.title: The key difference

compare_blocks.body:
In this fictional project, both editors have the same footage, brief, reviewer and deadline, and neither can add notes. Both have equal authority to propose changes.

Each row illustrates one preference or the shared P. Either editor can use the approach in either column. The examples cannot identify anyone’s type.

| Shared situation | ESFP: possible emphasis | INTP: possible emphasis | Preference illustrated |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Both make sense of the same scene | Explore what the scene needs by talking it through with a colleague | Explore what the same scene needs through private reflection | E/I: outward engagement or inward reflection |
| Both can keep an alternative before review | Keep more than one viable line open until feedback arrives | Keep the same viable lines open until the same feedback arrives | Shared P: both can leave room to revise |
| Both review the same pun and early feedback | The wording, timing and details viewers actually picked up | The pattern linking the two meanings and other ways to recreate it | S/N: concrete observations or patterns and possibilities |
| Both review a scene with the same slang | The words, delivery and immediate context on screen | How the expressions connect across scenes and what other readings they suggest | S/N: specific observations or connections beyond the immediate scene |
| The reviewer raises the same objection | Weigh what each available line would mean for viewers and for the portrayal of the character | Apply the same continuity and accuracy criteria to both available lines | T/F: effect on people and portrayal or consistent criteria |

compare_blocks.title: One-minute comparison

compare_blocks.body:
Imagine two subtitle editors who both keep an alternative line available before final review. A preference for openness can fit that choice, and so can a project brief that asks for options.

The shared P describes an approach to the outside world. In type dynamics, it means both profiles use an outward-facing perceiving function. Both can follow a glossary, meet a deadline and decide which line to submit.

The differing letters concern separate questions: where attention goes, which information stands out and what carries weight in a judgment. Someone can check a detail privately or discuss an abstract connection with colleagues.

### ### ESFP and INTP: weighing two ways to adapt the same pun

In a fictional kitchen scene, a character holds up a plate of food and says, “I’m a hot dish.” The joke links the literal hot meal with the character calling himself attractive. Two editors have the same footage and dialogue. Both need a one-line subtitle that can be read in about two seconds, with no room for a note.

For an English-language illustration, compare “I’m quite a catch” with “I’m the dish of the day.” The first makes the boast clear but loses the food image. The second keeps the food image and lets the shot carry part of the joke, but it may be less immediately clear as a boast.

One line of inquiry is what viewers could see and hear at the moment the line appears. Another is the connection between the two meanings and how a different phrase could recreate it. These illustrate S/N under the same conditions.

Either editor can check timing and look for another way to connect the meanings. Familiarity with the film, the intended audience and what the scene needs to communicate may guide the approach.

Show the alternatives to a few colleagues who have not seen the source. Ask what they understood and whether the line felt natural. Record those answers separately. The feedback can inform this edit and gives no evidence about a personality type.

### ### ESFP and INTP: how the two function stacks fit together

Both types have P, which points to an outward-facing perceiving function. For ESFP, S makes that function Se and E makes it dominant, supported by inward-facing Fi. For INTP, N makes the outward function Ne and I makes it auxiliary to inward-facing dominant Ti.

Under the convention used here, the stacks are Se–Fi–Te–Ni and Ti–Ne–Si–Fe. Pairing by family gives different orientations: Se with Si, Ni with Ne, Te with Ti, and Fi with Fe. The full order is different as well. In particular, ESFP’s dominant function takes in information and INTP’s dominant function evaluates it in the model.

The Foundation lists Thinking (Te or Ti) for ESFP’s tertiary function and Sensing (Se or Si) for INTP’s. Using Ti for ESFP or Se for INTP would produce an overlap with the other type’s dominant function. Function order does not set an order of action. See the [ESFP profile](/en/personality/esfp) and the [INTP profile](/en/personality/intp) for the individual descriptions.
compare_blocks.title: Why they are easily confused

compare_blocks.body:
The fictional examples below illustrate decisions with different constraints. For shared work, agree who can edit the subtitles, who can approve changes and who will review the finished version.

Both people can check how a line reads and whether the meaning is clear. When the checks point in different directions, use the agreed brief and the evidence available to decide what to keep.

### ### ESFP and INTP: what changes when notes are allowed?

In a fictional project, both editors review the same kitchen pun. The subtitle brief allows a single short line, while the written edition allows a note. Either editor could adapt the joke in the subtitle and explain the original wordplay in the written edition if that helps the reader.

Ask whether the plot depends on viewers understanding both meanings. If it does, a neighbouring line may carry meaning that will not fit in the subtitle. Changing the footage or adding text to the picture requires separate approval.

When reviewing two versions, record naturalness and comprehension separately. If one version reads more smoothly but loses a plot detail, check what the brief requires before choosing. That trade-off does not establish either editor’s type.

### ### ESFP and INTP: writing a sign for a food stall

In a fictional market, an aunt asks two people for a short sign for her stall. Both know what she cooks and how the food is prepared. They compare “Follow the aroma” with “Slow-cooked fresh daily.” The second only works if that is what the stall actually does.

Ask what people remember and what they understood about the food. A line can be memorable without stating what makes the stall different. A clear description can also be easy to forget.

If the sign has little space, the seller might use a short line on it and put a verified description on a label. Either person could suggest or check both.

### ### ESFP and INTP: delivering subtitles without notes

In a fictional project, the client tells both editors to remove the notes from the release version. Both have the same timing, footage and approval limits. First agree on the information a viewer must understand to follow the next scene.

Either editor can work that information into the line or let the surrounding dialogue or action carry it. Verify the result against the delivery brief. The task requirements explain the choice, and the choice alone cannot identify anyone’s type.

They both have a preference for openness to new information in the outside world. The model gives ESFP dominant Se and INTP auxiliary Ne.

faq_blocks.question: ### What does the P in both ESFP and INTP mean?

faq_blocks.answer:
Either could study the words and timing or look for a different way to connect the meanings. The choice can depend on what the plot needs and how much time the subtitle has on screen.

Ask reviewers what they understood and whether the line reads naturally. Discuss both findings against the brief. Those answers help refine the subtitle and do not identify an editor’s type.
faq_blocks.question: ### How might ESFP and INTP approach the same pun?

faq_blocks.answer:
Yes. Both can adjust a line by ear and trace its meaning carefully. The work may need both.

When reflecting on preferences, consider what information stood out in several comparable situations where you had a choice. A single case, or its order of actions, tells you little.
faq_blocks.question: ### Can an INTP rely on their ear and an ESFP insist on precision?

faq_blocks.answer:
Yes. The work requires skills such as revising dialogue, checking meaning and delivering to a brief. Match tasks to demonstrated skills and responsibility.

To explore the work, adapt a short fictional exchange and check it for clarity, timing and meaning. Compare what you want to practise with tasks in an actual localisation role.
faq_blocks.question: ### Can either type do subtitling or localisation work?

faq_blocks.answer:
State what each concern refers to. A line can sound awkward or leave out a link the audience needs. Both concerns can matter in the same edit.

Use the brief to distinguish what must be fixed from what can remain open to discussion. Agree who decides if the alternatives cannot satisfy both concerns.
faq_blocks.question: ### How can ESFP and INTP resolve a disagreement about a revision?

faq_blocks.answer:
Compare the questionnaire versions, languages and scoring. Consider what situations you used as examples when answering about E/I, S/N and T/F.

If the instrument explains its scores and cutoffs, use that guidance to interpret the difference. Two labels alone cannot show which score was close to a cutoff or which result is more representative.

sections.title: Quick answer

sections.body_md:
Imagine two subtitle editors who both keep an alternative line available before final review. A preference for openness can fit that choice, and so can a project brief that asks for options.

The shared P describes an approach to the outside world. In type dynamics, it means both profiles use an outward-facing perceiving function. Both can follow a glossary, meet a deadline and decide which line to submit.

The differing letters concern separate questions: where attention goes, which information stands out and what carries weight in a judgment. Someone can check a detail privately or discuss an abstract connection with colleagues.

### ### ESFP and INTP: weighing two ways to adapt the same pun

In a fictional kitchen scene, a character holds up a plate of food and says, “I’m a hot dish.” The joke links the literal hot meal with the character calling himself attractive. Two editors have the same footage and dialogue. Both need a one-line subtitle that can be read in about two seconds, with no room for a note.

For an English-language illustration, compare “I’m quite a catch” with “I’m the dish of the day.” The first makes the boast clear but loses the food image. The second keeps the food image and lets the shot carry part of the joke, but it may be less immediately clear as a boast.

One line of inquiry is what viewers could see and hear at the moment the line appears. Another is the connection between the two meanings and how a different phrase could recreate it. These illustrate S/N under the same conditions.

Either editor can check timing and look for another way to connect the meanings. Familiarity with the film, the intended audience and what the scene needs to communicate may guide the approach.

Show the alternatives to a few colleagues who have not seen the source. Ask what they understood and whether the line felt natural. Record those answers separately. The feedback can inform this edit and gives no evidence about a personality type.

### ### ESFP and INTP: how the two function stacks fit together

Both types have P, which points to an outward-facing perceiving function. For ESFP, S makes that function Se and E makes it dominant, supported by inward-facing Fi. For INTP, N makes the outward function Ne and I makes it auxiliary to inward-facing dominant Ti.

Under the convention used here, the stacks are Se–Fi–Te–Ni and Ti–Ne–Si–Fe. Pairing by family gives different orientations: Se with Si, Ni with Ne, Te with Ti, and Fi with Fe. The full order is different as well. In particular, ESFP’s dominant function takes in information and INTP’s dominant function evaluates it in the model.

The Foundation lists Thinking (Te or Ti) for ESFP’s tertiary function and Sensing (Se or Si) for INTP’s. Using Ti for ESFP or Se for INTP would produce an overlap with the other type’s dominant function. Function order does not set an order of action. See the [ESFP profile](/en/personality/esfp) and the [INTP profile](/en/personality/intp) for the individual descriptions.

sections.body_md:
In this fictional project, both editors have the same footage, brief, reviewer and deadline, and neither can add notes. Both have equal authority to propose changes.

Each row illustrates one preference or the shared P. Either editor can use the approach in either column. The examples cannot identify anyone’s type.

| Shared situation | ESFP: possible emphasis | INTP: possible emphasis | Preference illustrated |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Both make sense of the same scene | Explore what the scene needs by talking it through with a colleague | Explore what the same scene needs through private reflection | E/I: outward engagement or inward reflection |
| Both can keep an alternative before review | Keep more than one viable line open until feedback arrives | Keep the same viable lines open until the same feedback arrives | Shared P: both can leave room to revise |
| Both review the same pun and early feedback | The wording, timing and details viewers actually picked up | The pattern linking the two meanings and other ways to recreate it | S/N: concrete observations or patterns and possibilities |
| Both review a scene with the same slang | The words, delivery and immediate context on screen | How the expressions connect across scenes and what other readings they suggest | S/N: specific observations or connections beyond the immediate scene |
| The reviewer raises the same objection | Weigh what each available line would mean for viewers and for the portrayal of the character | Apply the same continuity and accuracy criteria to both available lines | T/F: effect on people and portrayal or consistent criteria |
| Only one version can be submitted | Weigh how each version handles the same audience concern | Weigh whether each version meets the same brief and preserves required information | T/F: effect on viewers or consistency with agreed criteria |

Experience with a title can make it easier to spot a reference. A project lead may be expected to contact the reviewer. Neither skill nor assignment determines who uses a particular approach.
sections.title: ESFP and INTP in one minute

sections.body_md:
The fictional examples below illustrate decisions with different constraints. For shared work, agree who can edit the subtitles, who can approve changes and who will review the finished version.

Both people can check how a line reads and whether the meaning is clear. When the checks point in different directions, use the agreed brief and the evidence available to decide what to keep.

### ### ESFP and INTP: what changes when notes are allowed?

In a fictional project, both editors review the same kitchen pun. The subtitle brief allows a single short line, while the written edition allows a note. Either editor could adapt the joke in the subtitle and explain the original wordplay in the written edition if that helps the reader.

Ask whether the plot depends on viewers understanding both meanings. If it does, a neighbouring line may carry meaning that will not fit in the subtitle. Changing the footage or adding text to the picture requires separate approval.

When reviewing two versions, record naturalness and comprehension separately. If one version reads more smoothly but loses a plot detail, check what the brief requires before choosing. That trade-off does not establish either editor’s type.

### ### ESFP and INTP: writing a sign for a food stall

In a fictional market, an aunt asks two people for a short sign for her stall. Both know what she cooks and how the food is prepared. They compare “Follow the aroma” with “Slow-cooked fresh daily.” The second only works if that is what the stall actually does.

Ask what people remember and what they understood about the food. A line can be memorable without stating what makes the stall different. A clear description can also be easy to forget.

If the sign has little space, the seller might use a short line on it and put a verified description on a label. Either person could suggest or check both.

### ### ESFP and INTP: delivering subtitles without notes

In a fictional project, the client tells both editors to remove the notes from the release version. Both have the same timing, footage and approval limits. First agree on the information a viewer must understand to follow the next scene.

Either editor can work that information into the line or let the surrounding dialogue or action carry it. Verify the result against the delivery brief. The task requirements explain the choice, and the choice alone cannot identify anyone’s type.
sections.title: ESFP and INTP at work and in daily life

sections.body_md:
Writing natural dialogue and keeping terminology consistent are both skills. Someone with either type can practise and use them.

Talking at length about a familiar topic or staying quiet in an unfamiliar room gives little information about E/I. The preference concerns the direction of attention and energy.

Perceiving describes a preference for leaving room for new information. It does not measure punctuality, care or reliability.

The same person may read one line aloud and analyse another closely. Experience, time and the difficulty of the material can explain the sequence.
sections.title: ESFP and INTP: avoiding misreads

sections.body_md:
If results differ, compare the questionnaire, version, language and scoring. Consider which situations you had in mind and what those situations required of you.

Pick several comparable decisions where you had a choice. Note where your attention went, what information stood out and what carried weight in your decision. Include situations where you worked differently.

Use the notes to describe your experience. They cannot determine your type or validate a test result.
sections.title: ESFP and INTP: how to keep observing

items.answer:
They both have a preference for openness to new information in the outside world. The model gives ESFP dominant Se and INTP auxiliary Ne.

Both can keep alternatives open and still meet the same brief. Whether a teammate keeps a second version does not show how they take in information or what they value in the final choice.
items.question: ### What does the P in both ESFP and INTP mean?

items.answer:
Either could study the words and timing or look for a different way to connect the meanings. The choice can depend on what the plot needs and how much time the subtitle has on screen.

Ask reviewers what they understood and whether the line reads naturally. Discuss both findings against the brief. Those answers help refine the subtitle and do not identify an editor’s type.
items.question: ### How might ESFP and INTP approach the same pun?

items.answer:
Yes. Both can adjust a line by ear and trace its meaning carefully. The work may need both.

When reflecting on preferences, consider what information stood out in several comparable situations where you had a choice. A single case, or its order of actions, tells you little.
items.question: ### Can an INTP rely on their ear and an ESFP insist on precision?

items.answer:
Yes. The work requires skills such as revising dialogue, checking meaning and delivering to a brief. Match tasks to demonstrated skills and responsibility.

To explore the work, adapt a short fictional exchange and check it for clarity, timing and meaning. Compare what you want to practise with tasks in an actual localisation role.
items.question: ### Can either type do subtitling or localisation work?

items.answer:
State what each concern refers to. A line can sound awkward or leave out a link the audience needs. Both concerns can matter in the same edit.

Use the brief to distinguish what must be fixed from what can remain open to discussion. Agree who decides if the alternatives cannot satisfy both concerns.
items.question: ### How can ESFP and INTP resolve a disagreement about a revision?

items.answer:
Compare the questionnaire versions, languages and scoring. Consider what situations you used as examples when answering about E/I, S/N and T/F.

If the instrument explains its scores and cutoffs, use that guidance to interpret the difference. Two labels alone cannot show which score was close to a cutoff or which result is more representative.
